list.listitem: All newborns should be screened for phenylketonuria (PKU) between 24 and 168 hours of life. A
A low-phenylalanine diet should be started upon diagnosis and continued throughout life. A

background.definition: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is a metabolic disorder characterized by the deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase, leading to an inability to metabolize the amino acid phenylalanine to tyrosine.

list.listitem: One new case per 10,000 to 15,000 live births.
More common in White and Native American children.
Autosomal recessive trait.
Most forms caused by mutations in the phenylalanine hydroxylase gene on chromosome 12q23.2.
Absence or deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase enzyme leads to an inability to metabolize phenylalanine to tyrosine.
Enzyme deficiency leads to a buildup of phenylalanine.
Rarely, may also be caused by a deficiency of tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), a required enzyme cofactor.
Demyelination and hypomyelination appear to be the neuropathology of both treated and untreated PKU.
All newborns should be screened between 24 and 168 hours of life (see ). A
Newborns with an abnormal screening test should have confirmatory testing with serum phenylalanine levels as soon as possible. C
Few new cases present clinically.
Differential diagnosis includes hyperphenylalaninemia.
Children with PKU who were not detected with newborn screening present with developmental delay in the first year of life.
They often have light skin coloring and blue eyes due to the relative lack of tyrosine, which interferes with melanin production.
They may also have a "mousy" or "musty" odor due to the buildup of phenylalanine.

In a study of 11 undiagnosed adults residing in Polish social welfare homes, common characteristics included poor physical growth (8/11), microcephaly (5/11), small thoracic circumference (9/11), and high risk of falls (6 high risk and 5 moderate risk).
Direct measurement of serum phenylalanine or amino acid levels confirms a positive screening test.
A DNA probe for the phenylalanine hydroxylase gene can also be performed for confirmation of a positive screening test or for prenatal diagnosis.
Severe illness, prematurity, use of total parenteral nutrition or blood products, or inadequate protein challenge prior to screening can reduce the sensitivity and specificity of the newborn screen.
Brain MRI diffusion-weighted imaging can be used to detect white matter abnormalities that are seen in patients with classical PKU.
Nearly all new cases are detected on routine newborn screening. Every state in the United States has a newborn screening campaign for PKU.
Direct measurement of serum phenylalanine or amino acid levels confirms a positive screening test (see ).
Treatment is by low-phenylalanine diet with consideration of medication.
Treatment with a low-phenylalanine diet should be started as soon as the diagnosis is made. A
Women with PKU who are at risk for pregnancy should maintain strict control of their phenylalanine levels to prevent neurologic damage to the fetus. A
Adjunct therapies, including pegvalise, sapropterin, and sepiapterin, are emerging for patients not at goal phenylalanine levels with low-phenylalanine diet alone. B

Tetrahydrobiopterin (sapropterin dihydrochloride; also called BH(4)) is considered an adjunct to the low-phenylalanine diet and has been shown in two trials to lower phenylalanine levels and increase protein tolerance in some patients with PKU; long-term data are limited evaluating its safety and efficacy. Adverse effects include headache, rhinorrhea (both at a frequency of ≥10%), pharyngolaryngeal pain, nasal congestion, cough, diarrhea, vomiting, and abdominal pain (all at a frequency of between 1% and 10%).
Oral sepiapterin is a sapropterin derivative that reduced serum phenylalanin levels in a phase 3 trial of patients with levels above goal while on a low-phenylalanine diet.
A 24-hour BH(4) loading test appears to be useful for screening patients with PKU for BH(4) responsiveness, as does phenylalanine hydroxylase genotype.

Pegvalise (pegylated phenylalanine ammonia lyase) reduces phenylalanine levels in adults with baseline levels >600 µmol/L. Neuropsychiatric symptoms improved in some patients whose phenylalanine levels improved. Dropout rates were 30% at 1 year and 70% at 2 years. Although most adverse effects were mild or moderate and included arthralgia, injection-site reactions or erythema, and headache, 12 of 261 participants experienced nonfatal anaphylaxis.

The mainstay of treatment is adherence to a low-phenylalanine diet.The low-phenylalanine diet requires restriction of almost all natural-protein sources and requires supplementation with phenylalanine-free amino acid sources. Many fruits and vegetables are freely allowed, but most dairy, meat, legumes and many grains are restricted. Because the low-phenylalanine diet is very low in protein, children with PKU may benefit from regular follow-up with a registered dietician or nutritionist.

Although there is evidence that a low-phenylalanine diet is effective in reducing blood phenylalanine levels and improving intelligence quotient and neuropsychological outcomes, there is uncertainty about the level of dietary restriction that should be maintained.

Infants may continue to breastfeed; however, as breast milk contains phenylalanine, supplementation with phenylalanine-free formula may be necessary. A retrospective study of infants diagnosed with PKU who were breastfed during the first year of life (mean 7.4 months) were found to have lower serum phenylalanine levels and higher monthly weight gain than infants who were initially breastfed and switched to phenylalanine-free formula upon diagnosis. Only infants who were strictly adherent to the diet were included in the study.

In a meta-analysis estimating the influence of age, phenylalanine level, and type of neuropsychological test on standardized differences in computer-based speed measurements between controls and patients with PKU, the effect of blood phenylalanine level on effect size was more pronounced in children and adolescents than in adults. The authors concluded that while recommendations for phenylalanine concentrations are likely appropriate for children, recommendations for adolescents may be too liberal.
Authors of a Cochrane review (4 studies, 250 participants) found IQ levels were higher in patients who continued the diet past adolescence, although these results were limited to a single study.

Dietary restriction, however, may continue to be important in adults; a small RCT with 9 subjects demonstrated that 4-weeks of phenylalanine supplementation, mimicking a normal diet, resulted in impairment in both sustained attention and mood during supplementation vs. placebo.

A small case series of 11 subjects with PKU given 4 days of a phenylalanine-free amino acid diet followed by 4 days of a diet with glycomacropeptide (an intact protein formed during cheese production that contains minimal phenylalanine) and limited amino acids found improved protein retention and phenylalanine utilization; most (10/11) preferred the glycomacropeptide diet.

There are only rare reports of adverse outcomes (eg, developmental delay) from inappropriate treatment with a restrictive diet of well children who were falsely identified as having PKU by early newborn screening programs.
Authors of a Cochrane review found insufficient data about the benefits of short- or long-term use of protein substitute in PKU.

As deficiency of the amino acid tyrosine has been suggested as a cause of some of the neuropsychological problems seen in children with PKU, Cochrane authors reviewed 3 trials of tyrosine supplementation including 56 subjects. No differences in outcomes were observed.
A small RCT of docosahexaenoic acid supplementation over 4 months for reproductive-age women with PKU did not show benefits on performance of cognitive tasks.

Other large neutral amino acids (LNAAs; valine, leucine, tyrosine and tryptophan, among others) use the same transport channels in the small intestine and brain as phenylalanine. Supplementation with LNAAs may decrease blood levels of phenylalanine and increase dopamine levels. Supplementation with LNAAs may also be used as adjunct therapy to the low-phenylalanine diet.
Children who adhere to the low-phenylalanine diet may achieve normal IQ levels, but they may still lag behind unaffected siblings. Performance on tests may fall if the diet is discontinued.

Adherence to a low-phenylalanine diet throughout life decreases the risk of intellectual disability and other neurologic sequelae. B However, neurocognitive, psychosocial, quality of life, growth, nutrition, bone pathology and maternal PKU outcomes appear to be suboptimal.

In one case series, median blood phenylalanine from children ages 0 to 6 years and 7 to 12 years were inversely associated with perceptual reasoning abilities and increased blood phenylalanine concentration negatively impacted specific areas of verbal comprehension abilities for those 0-6 years of age; intelligence was not affected by blood levels. Some evidence suggests improved intelligence outcomes in patients who continue the low-phenylalanine diet into adolescence.
Based on data from two large medical centers, children with PKU, especially girls, are more likely to be overweight and obese than children from the general population.

In a qualitative study of 20 patients age 8-23 years, patients with PKU did not report feeling ill but reported fear of stigmatization that prevented them from participating in social occasions during which food is shared.
Strict adherence to the PKU diet is also crucial for women who are pregnant because of the effects of phenylalanine on the brain development of the fetus.
Ideally phenylalanine intake and serum levels should be controlled for 3 months prior to conception and should continue throughout pregnancy.

Children born to mothers with uncontrolled PKU frequently exhibit microcephaly, low birth weight, and developmental delay, a condition known as maternal PKU syndrome. As PKU is an autosomal recessive condition, children born to mothers with PKU will not have PKU unless both parents have PKU.
